questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a hypopigmented patch over the left cheek with loss of sensation. Slit-skin smear shows acid-fast bacilli. Skin biopsy reveals well-formed granulomas with epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes cuffing the nerves. The bacillary index (BI) is 0. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) shows well-formed granulomas with Langhans giant cells, nerve destruction, and a negative BI (paucibacillary). Single or few hypopigmented patches with definite anesthesia are characteristic.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient on multidrug therapy for lepromatous leprosy develops sudden onset of painful erythematous nodules over the face, arms, and trunk with fever and malaise. CBC shows neutrophilia. This reaction is best managed with:
questions.exp: This is Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL / Type 2 reaction). Thalidomide is the drug of choice for recurrent/severe ENL in males. Prednisolone is used in females/children where thalidomide is contraindicated. Clofazimine can be used as a steroid-sparing agent but is not first-line for acute ENL.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on the right index finger with raised indurated edges. Regional lymphadenopathy is present. Gram stain of pus shows Gram-positive filamentous organisms. Sulphur granules are visible macroscopically. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Actinomycosis is caused by Actinomyces israelii, a Gram-positive filamentous, anaerobic organism. Sulphur granules (yellow colonies of organisms in pus) are pathognomonic. Nocardia is aerobic and also forms filaments but sulphur granules are uncommon.

questions.q: A 40-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with verrucous plaques over the dorsum of the right hand. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with microabscesses containing large spherical cells with thick double-contoured walls and horizontal septation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) shows verrucous plaques on exposed areas. Biopsy reveals muriform (sclerotic) bodies — round, brown, thick-walled cells with horizontal and vertical septa (Medlar bodies or copper pennies). These are pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent vesicles on the genital area. Culture is positive for HSV-2. She is now pregnant at 36 weeks. The most appropriate management to prevent neonatal herpes is:
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg three times daily from 36 weeks till delivery
Valacyclovir 1 g once daily from 36 weeks till delivery
No antiviral required if no active lesions at time of delivery
questions.exp: Suppressive acyclovir 400 mg TID (or valacyclovir 500 mg BD) from 36 weeks reduces viral shedding and recurrences at delivery. Caesarean section is indicated only if active lesions or prodrome are present at the onset of labor. Acyclovir 400 mg TID is the standard suppressive dose.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with painless shallow ulcers on the glans, followed by painful matted inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) with groove sign. The most likely diagnosis and causative organism are:
questions.exp: LGV is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The 'groove sign' (inguinal groove between superficial and deep lymph nodes) is characteristic. The primary lesion is a small painless ulcer, followed by painful buboes. Chancroid causes painful ulcers with painful buboes but no groove sign.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the penis for 2 weeks. VDRL is non-reactive. FTA-ABS is reactive. The best next step is:
opts: Treat as primary syphilis with benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM stat
Treat with doxycycline as the patient may be allergic to penicillin
Biopsy of the ulcer to confirm diagnosis
questions.exp: In primary syphilis, VDRL/RPR may be non-reactive (seroconversion takes 1–4 weeks after chancre appears), but treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPHA) are reactive earlier. A clinical chancre with reactive FTA-ABS confirms primary syphilis — treat with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters involving the oral mucosa and skin. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Immunofluorescence shows IgG deposits in a 'chicken wire' or 'honeycomb' pattern in the intercellular spaces of the epidermis. The target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmoglein 3 (and desmoglein 1 when skin is involved). Mucosal involvement is predominantly due to Dsg3 antibodies. DIF shows intercellular IgG (and C3) in a lace-like pattern. Dsg1 is targeted in pemphigus foliaceus (skin only, no mucosa).

questions.q: An elderly man presents with tense blisters on an erythematous base over the abdomen and thighs. Nikolsky's sign is negative. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister. DIF reveals linear C3 and IgG at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA is positive for NC16A domain antibody. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense blisters in elderly, negative Nikolsky sign. DIF: linear IgG and C3 at DEJ. The major antigen in BP is BP180 (collagen XVII), specifically the NC16A domain — detected by ELISA. EBA shows IgG at the floor of salt-split skin.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles over the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Biopsy shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophil microabscesses at dermal papilla tips. DIF reveals granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. He is found to have celiac disease on duodenal biopsy. The first-line treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillae (pathognomonic). Dapsone provides rapid symptom relief. Gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment and may allow dapsone to be tapered. Dapsone works by inhibiting neutrophil chemotaxis.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with known SLE develops a malar rash, photosensitivity, and arthralgias. ANA is positive with anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies. She develops discoid plaques on the scalp with follicular plugging and scarring alopecia. The histology of discoid lupus shows:
opts: Interface dermatitis with vacuolar degeneration and thickened basement membrane
Perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate without epidermal changes
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus shows interface (vacuolar/lichenoid) dermatitis with epidermal atrophy, follicular plugging, thickened PAS-positive basement membrane, and periadnexal mucin deposition. DIF shows 'lupus band' — granular IgG, IgM, C3 at the DEJ in involved skin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, and esophageal dysmotility. She also has calcinosis cutis. The most specific antibody in this condition is:
questions.exp: This is CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) — a form of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is the most specific antibody for this subtype. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash on the eyelids, Gottron's papules over the knuckles, and periungual erythema. CPK is markedly elevated. The most important investigation to screen for an underlying malignancy is:
opts: CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults has a significant association with underlying malignancy (ovarian, lung, colorectal cancers). CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis (and PET-CT in some guidelines) is the standard screening. The risk is highest in the first 2–3 years after diagnosis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasia on the nose. The lesion has been slowly growing for 2 years. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels. Biopsy reveals nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and stromal retraction artifact. The most common site and biological behavior are:
opts: Head and neck (nose); locally invasive, rarely metastasizes
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. Pearly/translucent papule with telangiectasia and arborizing vessels on dermoscopy is classic. Histology shows peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. BCC is locally invasive and destructive but rarely metastasizes (<0.5% of cases). Most common on the head and neck (nose being the most common site).

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer presents with a hyperkeratotic nodule on the lower lip. Biopsy shows islands of squamous cells with central keratin pearls invading the dermis. Perineural invasion is present. Regional lymph nodes are enlarged. This tumor is associated with:
opts: UV radiation and chronic actinic damage
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip is strongly associated with chronic UV (actinic) damage and smoking. SCC on lips, ears, and in immunosuppressed patients has higher metastatic potential. Perineural invasion is an aggressive feature. HPV 6/11 cause condylomata; HPV 16/18 are associated with Bowen's disease and SCC of genitalia.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing, deeply pigmented irregular nodule on the back that developed from a pre-existing mole over 3 months. Dermoscopy reveals atypical network, irregular dots and globules, and blue-white veil. The most important prognostic factor is:
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (vertical tumor depth in mm from the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell) is the single most important prognostic factor in melanoma and determines AJCC T staging. Clark level (anatomical level of invasion) is less reproducible. Mitotic rate is important for thin melanomas (T1b ≥1/mm²).

questions.q: A 55-year-old HIV-positive male presents with violaceous plaques on the lower limb. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and eosinophilic globules (PAS-positive intracytoplasmic inclusions). The causative virus is:
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8, also known as Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus, KSHV). It presents as violaceous plaques in immunosuppressed individuals (HIV/AIDS, organ transplant recipients). Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and eosinophilic globules.

questions.q: A patch test is performed on a 30-year-old woman suspected of having allergic contact dermatitis to nickel. The patch is applied for 48 hours and read at 48 hours and 96 hours. A positive reaction at 48 and 96 hours shows erythema, induration, and vesicles. The immunological mechanism underlying this reaction is:
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a classic Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized CD4+ Th1 cells (and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells). Patch test detects this. Nickel is the most common cause of ACD worldwide. Urticaria is Type I; drug-induced cytopenia is Type II; serum sickness is Type III.

questions.q: A Tzanck smear is prepared from the base of a fresh vesicle in a patient with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along a dermatomal distribution. The smear shows multinucleated giant cells. This finding is characteristic of:
questions.exp: Tzanck smear shows acantholytic cells in pemphigus and multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) in HSV, VZV, and varicella — all herpesviruses. It cannot distinguish between HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV. Molluscum shows Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies on smear.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male is started on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. After 2 weeks, he presents with pallor, jaundice, and dark urine. His CBC shows hemolytic anemia and Heinz bodies on peripheral smear. The most likely cause is:
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent methemoglobinemia and hemolysis in all patients, but severe hemolysis with Heinz bodies occurs particularly in patients with G6PD deficiency. Heinz bodies represent denatured hemoglobin precipitates. All patients starting dapsone should be screened for G6PD deficiency before treatment.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman with severe nodular acne is started on oral isotretinoin 0.5 mg/kg/day. The most important counseling before starting treatment is:
opts: Avoid sun exposure for the entire course
Use two forms of contraception starting 1 month before, during, and 1 month after treatment
Avoid dairy products to enhance absorption
Report any joint pains immediately as the drug must be stopped
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is highly teratogenic (Category X). Mandatory iPLEDGE-equivalent protocols require two forms of contraception starting 1 month before, throughout, and 1 month after treatment. Fasting lipids and LFTs are monitored. The drug is best absorbed with a fatty meal.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with plaque psoriasis covering 30% BSA is started on methotrexate. After 6 months of therapy, the cumulative dose reaches 1.5 g. What monitoring is recommended to detect hepatotoxicity?
opts: Liver biopsy at cumulative dose of 1.5 g
Procollagen III aminopeptide (PIIINP) levels and liver biopsy at 1.5–2 g cumulative dose
Liver enzymes every 2 weeks throughout treatment
questions.exp: EADV/BAD guidelines recommend monitoring with PIIINP (a fibrosis marker) and considering liver biopsy at cumulative doses of 1.5–2 g (some guidelines suggest 3.5–4 g). Liver biopsy at 1.5 g is traditional but current practice is guided by PIIINP levels. LFTs are monitored every 2–3 months during treatment.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated, silvery-scaly plaques over the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. The Auspitz sign and Koebner phenomenon are present. Biopsy shows regular acanthosis, parakeratosis, loss of granular layer, dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae, and Munro microabscesses. The pathogenetic mechanism primarily involves:
opts: Th17 cell activation and IL-17/IL-23 axis dysregulation
Th2 cell activation and IL-4/IL-13 excess
CD8+ cytotoxic T cell-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis
questions.exp: Psoriasis pathogenesis centers on the IL-23/Th17 axis. Dendritic cells produce IL-23, which drives Th17 cell differentiation. Th17 cells produce IL-17A and IL-22, causing keratinocyte hyperproliferation. This is the basis for biologics like secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) and ustekinumab (anti-IL-12/23). Th2 is predominantly atopic dermatitis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis is being considered for a biologic. He has a history of pulmonary tuberculosis treated 10 years ago. His chest X-ray shows fibrotic changes. His Mantoux test is 15 mm and IGRA is positive. The correct approach before starting anti-TNF therapy is:
opts: Treat with isoniazid prophylaxis for 9 months before starting anti-TNF therapy
No precaution needed as TB was treated 10 years ago
Repeat sputum AFB culture before decision
questions.exp: Anti-TNF agents (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) carry a risk of TB reactivation. IGRA-positive patients with prior TB history require latent TB treatment (isoniazid 300 mg/day for 9 months or rifampicin for 4 months) before starting anti-TNF therapy. IL-17 inhibitors have lower TB reactivation risk but isoniazid prophylaxis is still recommended by many guidelines.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with diffuse depigmentation of the skin over the face, hands, and perioral region. Wood's lamp examination shows enhanced depigmentation (chalk-white fluorescence). The histology would show:
opts: Decreased melanin in the basal layer with normal melanocyte count
Complete absence of melanocytes in the depigmented areas
Increased melanin in the basal layer with dermal incontinence
questions.exp: Vitiligo is characterized by complete absence/destruction of melanocytes in the depigmented patches on histology (Dopa staining confirms absence of melanocytes). Wood's lamp shows chalky white fluorescence. The pathogenesis involves autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (CD8+ T cells).

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills presents with symmetric hyperpigmentation over the cheeks, upper lip, and forehead that worsens in summer. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the hyperpigmentation. The first-line treatment is:
opts: Triple combination cream (hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) with strict photoprotection
questions.exp: Melasma (chloasma) is exacerbated by OCP, pregnancy, and UV. Wood's lamp accentuation indicates epidermal melasma (better prognosis). First-line treatment is the Kligman-Willis triple combination cream (hydroquinone + tretinoin + mild steroid) along with strict broad-spectrum sunscreen. OCP should be stopped if possible.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male smoker presents with palpable purpura over the lower legs, arthralgia, and peripheral neuropathy. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and hematuria. Serum cryoglobulins are positive. Hepatitis C serology is positive. The type of cryoglobulinemia is:
opts: Type II (mixed — monoclonal IgM + polyclonal IgG)
questions.exp: HCV-associated cryoglobulinemia is characteristically Type II (mixed essential cryoglobulinemia) — monoclonal IgM rheumatoid factor complexed with polyclonal IgG. It presents with the classic triad of purpura, weakness, and arthralgia (Meltzer's triad), plus systemic involvement. Type I is associated with myeloma/Waldenström's.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with SLE presents with painful ulcers on the legs, livedo reticularis, and a history of recurrent deep vein thrombosis and two pregnancy losses. Anticardiolipin antibodies are strongly positive. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) presents with arterial/venous thrombosis and obstetric morbidity (recurrent fetal losses). Skin manifestations include livedo reticularis, leg ulcers, and splinter hemorrhages. Anticardiolipin antibodies, anti-beta2-glycoprotein-I, and lupus anticoagulant are diagnostic. Treatment involves anticoagulation.

questions.q: A patient develops an acute photodermatitis 24 hours after ingesting a drug, presenting as erythema and blistering in sun-exposed areas with Mees' lines on nails and hyperpigmentation on photo-exposed sites. The mechanism is phototoxic. Which drug is most commonly implicated in this phototoxic reaction?
questions.exp: Doxycycline is the most common cause of drug-induced phototoxicity, particularly in clinical practice. Phototoxic reactions are dose-dependent, do not require prior sensitization, and occur in most individuals given sufficient UV exposure. Other common causes include fluoroquinolones, NSAIDs (naproxen, piroxicam), psoralens, and thiazides. Amiodarone causes blue-grey pigmentation.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with well-demarcated hypopigmented macules over the trunk and upper back with fine scales. KOH examination shows a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance (hyphae and spores). The causative organism and characteristic Wood's lamp finding are:
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and related species). KOH shows short curved hyphae and round spores ('spaghetti and meatballs' or 'bananas and grapes'). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green (or coppery-orange) fluorescence. Microsporum canis causes bright green fluorescence in tinea capitis; Corynebacterium causes coral red in erythrasma.
